chapter_theme: Leaving the schools of Vanji, Manimekalai finds Kovalan's father as a Buddhist ascetic there, hears how the Chera kings and her own ancestor took up the Buddha's teaching, that Kovalan's heaven still owes its evil deed and his release waits for the Buddha at Kapilai, and that drought-stricken Kanchi is her charge; she flies there, where the king, unable to tell whether his sceptre, austerity or women's chastity has failed, has built a copy of Manipallavam on a deity's word, and her bowl feeds every creature and brings back the rain before she casts off her disguise at Aravanar's feet.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, a Buddhist renunciant, still in an ascetic's borrowed form until the last line
Kovalan's father, the Puhar merchant now a Buddhist ascetic in Vanji (named here only as கோவலன் தாதை)
a Chera king of old, carver of the bow on the mountain, who fed the Dharma charanas in the Vanji grove
sky-going Buddhist sages returning from circling Samanoli in Lanka
Kovalan's namesake ancestor nine generations back, the Chera king's friend, who renounced and built a caitya in Vanji
the far-seeing ascetics of the Vanji caitya who foretell Puhar's drowning and Kovalan's release
the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, now in Kanchi
Manimekalai's companion, counted with Madhavi as her mothers (தாயர்)
the chamberlain of the Kanchi king
the Chola Ilangkilli, ally (துணை) of Killi, builder of the Bodhi caitya in Kanchi; taken here as the king of Kanchi, whom the Tamil calls மன்னன் and வேந்தன்
the great deity who appeared to the Kanchi king in the drought and foretold the maiden with the bowl
the hungry people of eighteen tongues and the beasts who gather at the bowl

manimekalai:28:1-16.reading: Seeking her mothers and Aravanar, Manimekalai leaves the schools' hall and passes through the outer quarters that ring the Chera's Vanji like besieging kings, where the waters of many uses all run together: hair-wash from the houses, the spent sandal water of the pleasure tanks, the scented sprays of the king's birthday, the water lay devotees pour on the monks' feet, the rain from charity pandals and the perfume-grinders' wash.
manimekalai:28:1-16.nuance: The list sets the monks' foot-washing (lines 11 and 12) among the city's ordinary waters: Vanji is shown as a city where lay Buddhist practice is already part of the daily scene, which prepares for the monastery she finds at line 72.
manimekalai:28:1-16.event: Manimekalai, looking for her mothers and Aravanar, passes the outer quarters of Vanji.

manimekalai:28:17-30.reading: Those mingled waters flow into the moat so that its crocodiles and fish lose their stink of flesh and its lotuses and lilies hum with bees, and beyond the moat girdling the city like a rainbow and the walls fitted with engines she reaches the bannered gate and goes in among the guards to the broad crowded street.
manimekalai:28:17-30.event: Manimekalai crosses the moat and walls of Vanji and enters by its gate.

manimekalai:28:31-45.reading: The narrator lists the streets of Vanji's trades: fish-sellers, salt-sellers, toddy-women, cake-makers, meat-sellers, potters, copper-, brass- and goldsmiths, carpenters, clay-modellers, painters, leather-workers, tailors, garland-makers, astrologers, bards who show the modes on the lute, and the shell-cutters and gem-workers.

manimekalai:28:46-61.reading: The catalogue goes on to the streets of the dancers who know both court and common styles, of the eight kinds of grain, of bards and panegyrists, of herders, weavers of fine cloth, gold-assayers and gem-sellers, the Brahmins' street, the streets of the king's and ministers' households, the halls, squares and crossroads, and the avenues where new elephants and horses are trained.

manimekalai:28:62-90.unit_note: Boundary moved from 85 to 90: the list of what Manimekalai tells the ascetic, which begins at line 74, runs to வந்த வண்ணமும் at line 90 and is closed by சொல்லினள் at 91; the core unit 62-85 cut it mid-list.
manimekalai:28:62-90.reading: Past artificial hills, groves and pools that the gods might leave heaven for, Manimekalai enters a monastery of the Buddha's preachers, fair as an Indra vihara where sky-walkers delight to dwell, bows at the feet of Kovalan's father, now a great ascetic, and recounts her life since the bowl: the gift of the bowl, her former birth shown by the seat, the goddess's comfort, her coming to Vanji after the sea took Puhar, and hearing the schools in a false form and finding none of them straight.
manimekalai:28:62-90.nuance: Lines 74 to 90 are a summary of kaathais 11 to 27 in her own report. The monastery is likened to an இந்திர விகாரம் with அந்தர சாரிகள் (69 to 70), the very words the Silappathikaram uses for the place where Kovalan's father renounced in Puhar. Line 85 keeps her in the பொய் உரு she took to hear the schools; she drops it only at line 245.
manimekalai:28:62-90.event: Manimekalai enters a Buddhist monastery in Vanji, bows to Kovalan's father, now an ascetic, and tells him her story.

claims.claim: the doctrines of the other schools are not sound and deserve no assent

manimekalai:28:91-100.unit_note: Units 86-99 and 100-119 replaced by 62-90, 91-100 and 101-119: the ascetic's sentence that begins at 93 ends only with மா தவம் புரிந்தேன் at line 100, which the core boundary at 99 split.
manimekalai:28:91-100.reading: Manimekalai asks the pure one whether seeing him is the fruit of her good deeds, and he answers that when he heard her father and mother had died in sorrow as their evil deeds ruined the city, he, fit for the loving dharma of the Sugata, knew household life for an illusion and wealth and body for things that do not last a moment, and took up the great austerity of unshaken dharma.
manimekalai:28:91-100.nuance: Her mother Madhavi is alive, so the தாய் who died with her father must be Kannaki, counted here as Manimekalai's mother. The Silappathikaram gives grief and a great gift as the cause of his renunciation; here he gives the reason in doctrine, that home is மாயம் and wealth and body do not stand, and he makes his fitness for the Sugata's dharma part of the cause.
manimekalai:28:91-100.event: Manimekalai asks the ascetic whether meeting him is her good deeds' fruit; he tells her he renounced on hearing of her parents' deaths.

claims.claim: Kovalan and Kannaki perished in sorrow through the evil deeds they themselves had done
household life is an illusion, and wealth and the body do not last even a moment

manimekalai:28:101-119.unit_note: Starts at 101 instead of 100 (see 91-100); ends at 119 as in the core.
manimekalai:28:101-119.reading: He tells her how he came to Vanji: long ago a Chera king of the Kuttuvar, who carved the bow on the mountain cleft, was in this grove with his women when Dharma charanas, sky-going sages returning from circling the peak Samanoli in Lanka, came down and sat on its rock; the king, by austerity done before, praised them, washed their lotus feet, fed them the six-flavoured food of four kinds from a vessel and bowed to them with his court.
manimekalai:28:101-119.nuance: The king is named only by his line and the epithet விடர்ச் சிலை பொறித்த வேந்தன், the bow carved in the cleft; the Tamil does not name him. The sages are தரும சாரணர், Buddhist counterparts of the Jain charanas of the Silappathikaram, and Samanoli (the peak now called Adam's Peak) is their place of worship. The king's welcome, feet washed and six tastes served, is the pattern Manimekalai follows at lines 239 to 243.
manimekalai:28:101-119.event: A Chera king of old meets sky-going Dharma charanas descending into this grove, washes their feet, feeds them and worships them.

claims.claim: honouring holy sages comes to a king through austerity done in a former life

manimekalai:28:120-137.reading: The charanas poured the Buddha's truth, the suffering of birth and the bliss of no birth, into the king's ear; Kovalan, the king's dear friend and Manimekalai's ancestor nine generations back, heard it too, gave away in seven days the crores he had earned himself, beyond his inheritance, became an ascetic and built a towering white caitya to the Sugata for the relief of all who come after; Kovalan's father came to worship it, heard its ascetics foretell that the sea would take Kaveripattinam, and stayed here.
manimekalai:28:120-137.nuance: This Kovalan is a namesake ancestor (ஒன்பது வழி முறை முன்னோன்), not Manimekalai's father; the epic gives the family a Buddhist past in Vanji. The distinction at lines 127 to 128 is exact: he gave away what he had earned, not what the ancestors had laid up. The prophecy of the flood (line 135) is why the ascetic is in Vanji and not in drowned Puhar.
manimekalai:28:120-137.event: Kovalan's ancestor hears the charanas, gives away his wealth, renounces and builds a caitya; Kovalan's father, come to worship there, is told Puhar will be drowned and stays in Vanji.

claims.claim: birth is suffering and freedom from birth is bliss, as the first teacher of dharma taught
a caitya to the Buddha is raised to end the distress of all who come after

manimekalai:28:138-149.reading: He gives the seers' word: her father, who went where his evil deed ripened, has appeared among the gods by the fruit of former austerity, yet must still eat that evil deed, and by the austerity he bore under the Bodhi of the earlier Buddha he will take up austerity again and with his beloved reach release by hearing the Lord's dharma at Kapilai; understanding this, the ascetic resolves to hear that dharma on that day too, and asks whether she did not learn her own nature from Thuvathikan in the pillar.
manimekalai:28:138-149.nuance: Merit and evil deed run side by side here: heaven is earned and the evil deed is not cancelled by it, only deferred. Lines 141 to 142 are compressed (முன்னவன் போதியில் நல் அறம் தாங்கிய தவத்தால் தான் தவம் தாங்கி), and whose earlier Bodhi is meant is not fixed. Line 148 carries more words than an akaval line and may join two lines.
manimekalai:28:138-149.event: The ascetic reports the seers' prophecy of Kovalan's heaven, remaining karma and future release at Kapilai, and vows to hear the Buddha then himself.

claims.claim: an evil deed that has ripened must still be eaten even by one reborn among the gods for former merit
austerity kept under a former Buddha's Bodhi bears fruit in a later birth
release is reached by hearing the Buddha's dharma

manimekalai:28:150-161.reading: He tells her that Aravanar declared Kanchi the ground of her dharma and went there, her mothers following, and that because the Kanchi country has lost its rain and its people are dying, its ascetics, finding none to give them alms, have come to Vanji; so it is her duty, medicine of lives, to appear in that land like a rain cloud and save it.
manimekalai:28:150-161.nuance: The drought is told first through its effect on the monks: with no givers left, even austerity must migrate. The charge repeats Thuvathikan's foretelling in kaathai 21 almost line for line (பொன் எயில் காஞ்சி, மழை வளம் கர).
manimekalai:28:150-161.event: The ascetic tells Manimekalai that Aravanar and her mothers have gone to drought-struck Kanchi and charges her to go and save it.

claims.claim: one who holds the means to feed a starving land is bound to go and protect it

manimekalai:28:162-183.unit_note: Boundary moved from 182 to 183: the chamberlain's report that begins at 179 ends with மா மழை போல்' என at line 183.
manimekalai:28:162-183.reading: Manimekalai bows, takes the bowl, rises west of Vanji and flies north to Kanchi, which lies desolate though rich as Indra's city fallen to earth; heart melting, she circles its walls, comes down in the city's centre, worships the caitya that Ilangkilli, ally of Killi, made for the Lord of the Bodhi, and goes to a grove to the south-west; a chamberlain tells the king that Kovalan's daughter, keeper of the virtuous vows, has appeared in the Dharmadavanam with the Amudhasurabhi like a great rain cloud.
manimekalai:28:162-183.nuance: The chamberlain names her by her father (கோவலன் மடந்தை) and her vows (குணவதம்), not by her courtesan mother. The Tamil names Ilangkilli as the builder of the caitya; it does not here name the reigning king of Kanchi, though the epic's tradition makes him that king.
manimekalai:28:162-183.event: Manimekalai flies to drought-stricken Kanchi with the bowl, worships at Ilangkilli's caitya, and a chamberlain reports her arrival to the king.

manimekalai:28:184-206.unit_note: Units 183-203 and 204-219 replaced by 184-206 and 207-219: the king's speech, which begins at 187, quotes the deity to புனைமின் at 204 and ends with அவ் இடம் காட்ட at 206; the core boundary at 203 cut the deity's words.
manimekalai:28:184-206.reading: The king and his counsellors, saying the pillar image's words have all come true, go to her, and he tells her that, not knowing whether his sceptre had bent, austerity had failed, or women's chastity had fallen short, so that the whole land was in want, he was bewildered when a great deity appeared and told him not to grieve: by his own high austerity a maiden would come, her great bowl would save the land, at her grace Indra would send rain, and he should build a pool and grove as if Manipallavam with its Gomukhi pool had come here; this, he says, showing her the place, is what they made.
manimekalai:28:184-206.nuance: The king tries the three causes the tradition gives for failed rain, the bent sceptre, failed austerity and failed chastity, and the deity answers none of them: it does not say which was at fault but points to a remedy, the renunciant's bowl, and credits the king's own austerity for bringing her. The words அலத்தல்காலை ஆகியது and நலத்தகை repeat Aravanar's lament over Puhar's famine in kaathai 15. How the king knows the pillar image's words (185) is not told here.
manimekalai:28:184-206.event: The Kanchi king goes to Manimekalai and tells how a deity, in the drought, foretold her coming and bade him build a replica of Manipallavam's pool and grove, which he shows her.

claims.claim: a land's rain fails when the king's sceptre bends, when austerity fails, or when women's chastity falls short
a ruler's own austerity can bring a saviour to his stricken land

manimekalai:28:207-219.reading: Seeing the grove like the island, she rejoices and takes it for the seat that showed her former birth; a lotus seat of the Virtuous One is laid out in due form, a fitting shrine is made for Deepathilakai and the great goddess Manimekala to be worshipped, the king holds festival, and she worships, sets the Amudhasurabhi, medicine for the disease of hunger, on the lotus seat, and calls, let all living beings come.
manimekalai:28:207-219.nuance: Who lays out the seat at lines 210 to 211 is not clear: அறவோன் may be the Buddha whose seat it is, with the king as the builder, or the builder himself. On Manipallavam the bowl rose from the pool once a year into a fit hand; here it is set on the replica seat and offered to every creature.
manimekalai:28:207-219.event: A replica of the Buddha's seat and a shrine to the two goddesses are made in the Kanchi grove; Manimekalai sets the bowl on the seat and calls all beings to come.

manimekalai:28:220-233.reading: At her word the peoples of the eighteen tongues, the blind, deaf and lame, the uncared-for, the mute and the sick, the vow-keeping ascetics, the hungry and the destitute, with countless herds of beasts, all gather, and the bowl becomes life's medicine to all who eat, its plenty swelling like the fruit of alms laid in great ascetics' hands and like seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools, until the rain's work too brings abundance.
manimekalai:28:220-233.nuance: The list gives the disabled, the ascetics and the animals alike; the bowl makes no distinction of birth or species. Two images of increase are set side by side: the merit of alms given to ascetics and the harvest of well-sown seed, both depending on conditions. வசித் தொழில் at line 233 is a rare word; read as the work of rain, it fulfils the deity's promise at lines 196 to 197.
manimekalai:28:220-233.event: All the hungry people and animals of the land gather and eat from the bowl, and rain returns.

claims.claim: alms placed in the hands of great ascetics yield growing fruit, as seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools

manimekalai:28:234-245.reading: As the people go praising the maiden who cured the disease of hunger, her mothers and Aravana Adigal, who drives away what is not right, come to the hall of charity of the city's mother of lives; she bows at his feet, washes them, seats him, serves the six-flavoured food of four kinds in its hour, offers betel and camphor, prays that the dharma in her heart may come true, and, casting off her illusory form, bows down.
manimekalai:28:234-245.nuance: மாயை விட்டு is the dropping of the borrowed ascetic's form she took to hear the schools (பொய் உரு, line 85; the patikam's பொய் உருக் களைந்து). Her prayer வாய்வது ஆக என் மனப்பாட்டு அறம் turns into her own vow the blessing Aravanar is foretold to give in kaathai 21. She honours her teacher as a lay giver before she takes vows in kaathai 29.
manimekalai:28:234-245.event: Aravanar and her mothers arrive at the hall of charity; Manimekalai washes their feet, feeds them, prays for her dharma and casts off her disguise.

links.note: Maadalan reports that Kovalan's father, grieving, gave great gifts and renounced in Puhar's Indra viharas before the sky-walkers; in the Manimekalai the same man, in a Vanji monastery likened to an Indra vihara of sky-walkers, gives his own reason.
links.teaches: The Silappathikaram tells his renunciation as a grief-driven act seen from outside; the sequel gives it from inside as doctrine, home as illusion and wealth and body as passing, so one renunciation is told first as a mourning and then as a conversion.

links.note: The quatrain has the best of people renounce home and wealth after slow reflection on impermanence; the ascetic renounces when the news of his son's death by evil deeds reaches him.
links.teaches: The pairing shows impermanence learned two ways: the quatrain's sage reasons his way to it, while the epic's merchant has it forced on him by bereavement and only then states it as the doctrine.

gains.a: the ascetic's turn gains a known ethical type, the renouncer who sees nothing stands, against which his grief-driven timing stands out
gains.b: the quatrain's unhurried reflection gains a case where the same insight comes suddenly, through a son's ruin

links.note: The Akananuru remembers Cheralathan who carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped tribute at Maanthai; the epic's Chera of the carved bow feeds Buddhist sages in a Vanji grove. The Tamil shares only the epithet of the carved bow and the Chera line, not a name.
links.teaches: Holding them together shows the epic borrowing a Sangam conqueror's epithet to give Vanji's Buddhism a royal founder, turning the king remembered for hoarded tribute into a king remembered for a gift to monks.

gains.a: the nameless king of the epic gains a Sangam identity as the bow-carving conqueror, which the epic leaves unstated
gains.b: the poem's image of the conqueror's hoard gains a later legend in which the same line gives food rather than piles treasure

links.note: The Vanji ascetics foretell that the sea will take Kaveripattinam; in kaathai 25 the sea swallows it by the Manimekala goddess's curse and the ascetic and the mothers go to Vanji.
links.teaches: The flood of Puhar is given two causes in the epic, a prophecy the seers already knew and a goddess's curse on a negligent king, so foreknowledge and a moral cause sit together without either cancelling the other.

links.note: Kannaki's image says the two went to the gods by former good deeds, the evil deed will still come, and they will wander until the Buddha appears at Kapilai; the Vanji seers foretell the same and add that Kovalan's merit came from austerity under an earlier Buddha's Bodhi.
links.teaches: The second witness confirms the first and supplies its missing cause, so the couple's heaven is traced to a past Buddhist austerity, not to Kannaki's chastity alone.

links.note: The Silappathikaram ends Kannaki's story with her ascent in the gods' car with Kovalan; the Manimekalai says that this heaven only defers the evil deed, and that release waits for the Buddha at Kapilai.
links.teaches: Read together, the apotheosis that closes the first epic becomes a way station in the second: a Buddhist sequel re-reads the pathini's reward as a heaven still bound by deeds.

links.note: Both hold that heaven belongs to the round of deeds; Tirumular frees the soul from heaven, hell and earth by grace, while the seers have Kovalan freed by hearing the Buddha's dharma after he has eaten his deed.
links.teaches: The two agree that heaven is no escape from karma and part exactly on the way out: Saiva release is given by grace, while the Buddhist release comes after the deed is spent and the teaching heard, with no giver.

gains.a: the seers' prophecy gains a rival account of release that makes plain it involves no god
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a named case, Kovalan in heaven still owing his deed, of the soul turned through heaven by karma

links.note: The couplet says that without rain neither giving nor austerity lasts; the ascetic reports that Kanchi's ascetics, finding no almsgivers in the drought, have left for Vanji.
links.teaches: The epic shows the couplet's rule as a chain: the drought ends giving first, and austerity, which lives on gifts, then has to leave the land.

gains.a: the monks' migration gains a stated principle that explains why drought drives out ascetics
gains.b: the couplet gains the mechanism it leaves implicit, that austerity fails because giving fails

links.note: Thuvathikan foretold the drought in Kanchi and that she would bring rain there with the bowl; Kovalan's father now gives the same charge and asks whether she did not learn it from Thuvathikan.
links.teaches: A goddess's foretelling becomes a human teacher's command, so her mission to Kanchi rests on two witnesses, one divine and one from her own family.

links.note: The couplet says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; the Kanchi king names the bent sceptre as only one of three possible causes and cannot tell which holds.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's law into a king's anxious self-examination, and then sets it aside: the deity names no fault and sends a renunciant's bowl instead of a reform of rule.

gains.a: the king's question gains its source, the received rule that ties rain to the sceptre
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the rule cannot be applied, since the drought comes and the ruler cannot find his fault

links.note: The couplet gives the chaste wife power to bid rain fall; the king asks whether failed chastity among women withheld it.
links.teaches: The pair shows the couplet's power run in reverse: if a wife's chastity can command rain, the community's women can be suspected when it fails, and the epic records the suspicion without confirming it.

gains.a: the king's third cause gains the couplet's claim that underlies it
gains.b: the couplet gains its darker corollary, that drought can be laid at women's door

links.note: In Puhar Aravanar asks whether Indra or the king of the just sceptre is at fault for the famine, in the words அலத்தல்காலை ஆகியது; the Kanchi king uses the same words about his own land and adds women's chastity.
links.teaches: The question first put by the teacher about another's kingdom is put by a king about himself, and both times the epic's answer is the bowl, not a judgment on the ruler.

links.note: In Puhar she appears with the bowl like a rain cloud over a scorched bamboo forest; in Kanchi the chamberlain says she has come like a great rain cloud.
links.teaches: The simile becomes literal: in Puhar the cloud is only food for the hungry, while in Kanchi her coming brings real rain to a land in drought.

links.note: On Manipallavam the bowl rises from the Gomukhi pool before the Buddha's seat once a year into a fit hand; in Kanchi the king builds a copy of the pool and seat and she sets the bowl on it for all beings.
links.teaches: The holy island is reproduced in a royal city, and the bowl that came out of it to one worthy hand is now placed on the copy of the seat and offered to everyone.

links.note: The couplet asks whether the host who feeds guests need even sow his field; the epic likens the bowl's plenty to alms in ascetics' hands and to seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools.
links.teaches: Both make feeding others a kind of sowing, but the couplet promises the giver's field yields unsown, while the epic makes the yield depend on conditions, the worth of the receiver among them.

gains.a: the epic's image gains a contrast that shows how conditional its sowing is
gains.b: the couplet's unconditional promise gains a rival view in which a gift's fruit depends on where and how it is sown

links.note: Thuvathikan foretold that her bowl of dharma would give rain's plenty to a parched world; here the bowl feeds Kanchi and the rain returns.
links.teaches: The fulfilment shows the epic treating feeding as the cause of rain, reversing the usual order in which rain must come before there is food to give.

links.note: Aravanar, in Thuvathikan's foretelling, blesses her with வாய்வதாக நின் மனப்பாட்டு அறம்; at Kanchi she says it of herself, வாய்வது ஆக என் மனப்பாட்டு அறம்.
links.teaches: The teacher's blessing becomes the pupil's own vow in the same words, marking the point where she stops being foretold and begins to will her path.

links.note: The Chera king washes the charanas' feet and serves them six-flavoured food of four kinds; Manimekalai washes Aravanar's feet and serves the same.
links.teaches: The lay gift that founded Buddhism in Vanji is repeated by Manimekalai in Kanchi, so her entry into the order is staged as the same act of royal hospitality to monks.

source_issues: Line 148 (நின்னது தன்மை அந் நெடு நிலைக் கந்தில் துன்னிய) is longer than an akaval line and may join two lines of the edition.
Line 181 had a stray HTML mark removed by the core build (flag printed by show).
